public_rationale: The core of the claim is that Operator could not control a computer consistently and was not ready for general use. OpenAI's own evidence backs that. OpenAI released Operator only as a research preview and said it did not expect it to 'perform reliably in all scenarios' (e1). On full computer-control tasks it succeeded 38.1% of the time, against 72.4% for humans (e2). Early independent testers found it made too many mistakes to rely on without constant supervision (e3). 'Barely works' overstates things: it scored 87% on simpler web tasks and went 10 for 10 on some trials (e4). Still, the claim's substance, inconsistent and not ready, holds. The market remark is his opinion and is not graded.
limitations: 'Barely works' is stronger than the evidence; on simple web tasks Operator often succeeded.
Benchmarks and trial results come mainly from OpenAI itself; the independent evidence is anecdotal.

statement.excerpt: As a product, Operator barely works. As I covered a few weeks ago, this product — which claims to control your computer and does not appear to be able to do so consistently — is not even close to ready for prime time, nor do I think it has a market.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: at launch (late January to late February 2025), Operator often failed to finish tasks, its reliability varied widely by task, and it was not reliable enough for ordinary users to trust it without supervision.
'Nor do I think it has a market' is the speaker's opinion and is not graded.
Target period: from Operator's launch on 2025-01-23 to the post date, 2025-02-24, the version he described.
criteria.support_condition: Benchmark results, company disclosures or hands-on tests from the period show low or inconsistent task success, or say it is not reliable without supervision.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence from the period shows Operator reliably completed most real-world tasks it was given, at a level fit for general use.

evidence.excerpt: As with any early-stage technology, we don’t expect CUA to perform reliably in all scenarios just yet.
evidence.explanation: OpenAI itself said the model behind Operator was not yet reliable across scenarios and released it only as a research preview, which supports 'not consistently' and 'not ready for prime time'.

evidence.excerpt: OSWorld⁠(opens in a new window) is a benchmark that evaluates models’ ability to control full operating systems like Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS. In this benchmark, CUA achieves 38.1% success rate.
evidence.explanation: On full computer-control tasks, the model succeeded only 38.1% of the time, against 72.4% for humans on the same page. That directly supports 'does not appear to be able to do so consistently'.

evidence.excerpt: However, it still makes too many mistakes for human users to rely on it for important tasks without constant supervision.
evidence.explanation: An independent roundup of early user tests found Operator too error-prone to rely on without constant supervision, which supports 'not ready for prime time'.

evidence.excerpt: CUA achieved a 58.1% success rate on WebArena and an 87% success rate on WebVoyager for web-based tasks.
evidence.explanation: On simpler web tasks the model succeeded 87% of the time, and some trials on the same page were 10 out of 10. This cuts against the strongest wording, 'barely works', though not against 'not consistently'.
